title: UPDATE: Hawley's STOP Flock Abuse Act Proposes Limits on AI Plate Surveillance
summary:
A new federal bill aims to stop the automatic creation of digital footprints for millions of American drivers by restricting the scope of license plate networks. Senator Josh Hawley introduced the STOP Flock Abuse Act on September 30 to curb AI-enhanced surveillance and protect citizens from unauthorized tracking. The legislation follows a Senate hearing where the company Flock admitted its cameras can identify bumper stickers and capture images of passengers inside vehicles.

The bill responds to widespread reports of misuse, including charges against 5 Indianapolis police officers for tracking romantic partners, with one officer allegedly searching more than 1,000 plates. Other vulnerabilities include the sale of law enforcement accounts by Russian dark web vendors and wrongful arrests that jailed an Army veteran for 30 days and another woman for 13 days. In response to these concerns, Boston disabled its cameras and an Arizona sheriff canceled his county's contract with the firm.

‼️ Five Indianapolis police officers have been charged over Flock license plate camera searches, accused of tracking romantic partners, spouses and women they met in public, with prosecutors alleging one officer searched more than 1,000 plates and used the data to engineer encounters.

Marion County Prosecutor Ryan Mears called the audit behind the charges "just the beginning" of Flock-related cases.

selectedTweets.text:
Woman falsely accused of causing a fatal car crash with Flock camera data:

On October 4th, 2025, I spent the day with my mom at my apartment in Florida. At approximately 1:04 am, 3 deputies from the sheriff's office arrived looking for me. I gave them my information showing where I had been. A Flock automated license plate camera had captured my Dodge Durango 2-3 miles west of the crash scene. Despite this, the investigation continued to focus on me. I was placed in solitary confinement for approximately 3 and a half days.

selectedTweets.bestBit: If we rely on private camera networks to continuously log the habits of innocent Americans without a warrant, we are paving the way to an AI-driven surveillance state
selectedTweets.text:
Arizona Sheriff who ended the Flock camera contract in his county:

If we rely on private camera networks to continuously log the habits of innocent Americans without a warrant, we are paving the way to an AI-driven surveillance state. We must establish clear boundaries for automatic license plate readers. We cannot wait for a future Supreme Court ruling to correct AI overreach. We must protect the Fourth Amendment today.

selectedTweets.text: Cybersecurity researcher: I found that Flock did not require their clients to use multi-factor authentication. This led me to find Flock law enforcement accounts for sale by a Russian vendor on a dark web marketplace. In addition to this, we found insufficiently protected sensitive information stored on Flock cameras, including photos, license plate data, logs, API keys, passwords, and communications.
